entry.title: Room for their own movement
entry.invitation: The authors make room for the baby’s own awake movement, with comfort and help close by.
entry.summary: The authors favor awake movement that the baby initiates, with room to explore, help when needed, and no propping into sitting or standing before they can get there themselves.
entry.cue: Notice how your baby moves now, what catches their attention, and when effort becomes frustration.
detail: Davies and Uzodike describe a prepared space where a baby can explore their own movements. A nearby object may invite a reach or a change of direction; the point is to follow the baby’s present interest and pace.

Their caution is about propping a baby into sitting or standing. They separately describe awake time on both the back and tummy, while noticing discomfort and changing things or picking the baby up when needed.

When effort turns to frustration, they describe coming closer and offering enough help for the baby to continue. Their activity ages are guides, and they explicitly welcome seeking support for developmental concerns.

entry.title: Let them know before a pickup
entry.invitation: When a pickup can wait, let them know and pause for their response.
entry.summary: When a pickup can wait, come into view, say what you have in mind, and pause for a response. Necessary care or protection still calls for gentle action.
entry.cue: You are about to pick your baby up, and there is time to make it an exchange.

entry.title: Make a mark
entry.invitation: Paper and an easy-to-hold crayon, with no picture to copy.
entry.summary: Offer paper and a chunky pencil or crayon that makes an easy mark. Your child can explore lines and movement without making a picture of anything.
entry.cue: Notice an interest in making marks and whether the drawing material is comfortable to hold.
detail: Protect the table and leave the marks to your child. If you draw together, use your own paper. When showing the material, a loose line or squiggle leaves plenty for them to discover.

entry.title: “I want to do it” when it is time to dress
entry.summary: Let your child try a small part of dressing, with help when it is wanted or needed. The amount they want to do can change from day to day.
entry.cue: They may reach for their clothes, resist help, or ask you to do something they managed yesterday.
detail: Davies suggests easy openings and clothes that allow movement, with a limited choice of seasonally suitable things within reach. Elastic waists and a roomy neck opening are examples.

Break dressing into small parts. You might put a shirt over their head and leave the sleeves for them to try, or hold the back of a shoe while they put a foot in. Offer a little help when they are becoming frustrated.
When you must leave, acknowledge the wish to do it alone and explain that you will help finish. Davies keeps gentle handling and connection alongside the adult’s time boundary.

entry.title: Begin with your voice
entry.invitation: Say a few words, then wait for a sound or gesture.
entry.summary: Use your baby’s name and tell them what is happening. Pause so a sound or gesture can become part of the conversation.
entry.cue: You are holding or caring for your baby, with a moment to talk and listen.
detail: A bath about to begin, the part of the body being washed, or the room you are entering can give you something to talk about. Use the words you know and speak gently.

Let your baby see your face. After saying something, wait and notice their response. You might echo a sound or answer a gesture, then leave another pause. The book treats these early exchanges as conversation.
If your baby has an older sibling, another conversation can begin while that child plays: with the baby awake, talk about what their sibling is doing.

entry.invitation: A small jug, a little water, and a turn to pour—with help nearby.
entry.summary: If your child is interested in pouring and can manage a small jug, offer a little water with a cloth nearby. Stay available to help.
entry.cue: Notice an interest in tipping, filling, or pouring, and whether the jug feels manageable in their hands.
detail: A small amount of water makes the invitation easier to share. Davies includes pouring in ordinary family life, with a little jug and something ready for spills.
Show the movement slowly, then leave room for a turn. Your child may want to repeat just the pouring or the wiping. You can help with the rest.
steps: Set out a small jug with a little water, a glass, and a cloth or sponge for spills.
Show one slow pour, then offer a turn.
Wipe up together when needed.

entry.title: Make a mark
entry.invitation: Paper and an easy-to-hold crayon, with no picture to copy.
entry.summary: Offer paper and a chunky pencil or crayon that makes an easy mark. Your child can explore lines and movement without making a picture of anything.
entry.cue: Notice an interest in making marks and whether the drawing material is comfortable to hold.
detail: Protect the table and leave the marks to your child. If you draw together, use your own paper. When showing the material, a loose line or squiggle leaves plenty for them to discover.
When your child looks to you, you can describe a line or color you notice, or ask if they would like to tell you about it. The drawing need not stand for a recognizable object.
steps: Put out paper and a chunky pencil or crayon that glides easily.
If needed, show a loose line on your own paper.
Let your child explore, with more paper available if they want another turn.

entry.title: A place for shoes
entry.invitation: A familiar basket and one small part of getting ready.
entry.summary: A reachable basket gives shoes a familiar home. Invite your child to fetch them or put them away with you.
entry.cue: Notice whether your child looks for their shoes or wants to help when you leave or come home.
detail: Choose a consistent place your child can reach. A seat nearby can make putting shoes on and taking them off easier to join.
Show the small movements slowly. Fetching one shoe or returning it to the basket may be their part today; you can carry the other. On another day, more help may be welcome.
steps: Keep shoes in one reachable basket or on a shelf.
Invite your child to bring a shoe when you get ready.
Show where it belongs when you return, and put the shoes away together.

entry.title: “I want to do it” when it is time to dress
entry.summary: Let your child try a small part of dressing, with help when it is wanted or needed. The amount they want to do can change from day to day.
entry.cue: They may reach for their clothes, resist help, or ask you to do something they managed yesterday.
detail: Davies suggests easy openings and clothes that allow movement, with a limited choice of seasonally suitable things within reach. Elastic waists and a roomy neck opening are examples.

Break dressing into small parts. You might put a shirt over their head and leave the sleeves for them to try, or hold the back of a shoe while they put a foot in. Offer a little help when they are becoming frustrated.
When you must leave, acknowledge the wish to do it alone and explain that you will help finish. Davies keeps gentle handling and connection alongside the adult’s time boundary.

entry.title: Remember something you did together
entry.invitation: Bring a shared moment into conversation, and listen for their part of the story.
entry.summary: When your child is using some spoken language, bring a shared experience into an ordinary conversation. Leave time for the part they want to tell.
entry.cue: Your child uses some spoken language and has an experience you can remember together.
detail: While preparing food or doing the laundry, you might remember planting something together and wonder where you put it or what you used. Davies describes this as a natural conversation, rather than a round of questions to answer correctly.

Listen without finishing the sentence for them. If their meaning is unclear, invite them to show you. Naming objects for a child is different from testing whether they know the names; the book reserves the formal naming test for children over 3.

entry.title: Spray, wipe, and try again
entry.invitation: A little water, a squeegee, and a window-cleaning turn to share.
entry.summary: Share a window-cleaning turn with water, a small squeegee, and a cloth. Your child may want to repeat just the spraying or wiping while you help with the rest.
entry.cue: Your child wants to copy a spraying or wiping movement.
detail: Davies groups the window tools together so they are ready for the job. Her detailed example uses a spray bottle with a cup of water, a small squeegee, and a chamois or cloth; adding vinegar is optional in the book.
Show a slow movement and let your child try the part that interests them. Put out only as much as you want to clean up, keep a cloth ready, and stop before the shared work becomes overwhelming.
